title: Course Overview and Math Recap
summary: Frame a modeling problem by choosing what to predict, what can change, and what data can test the prediction.
text: The modeling question A useful dynamic model predicts how a system evolves from an initial state under an input. The level of detail depends on which output you need. Worked example · Choose what to measure To study ride comfort after a bump, use the road height as the input and the car body’s vertical acceleration as the output. If the car starts on a level road at equilibrium, set its initial displacement and velocity relative to that equilibrium to zero. Compare the predicted acceleration with an accelerometer on the body. From a physical system to a prediction Identify the system boundary, input, output, and relevant states. Choose assumptions, signs, and units. Draw the forces or flows where appropriate. Combine the governing balance with component laws to get equations. Solve or simulate, then check the result against a limiting case and data. Try the model boundary. If the question changes from rider comfort to tire contact, keep the same road input and choose tire deflection as an output. A single body accelerometer cannot directly measure that deflection. Follow the wheel and body over a bump. Modeling versus analysis Modeling produces the equations. Analysis explains what those equations predict, including equilibrium, transients, oscillation, and stability. A comparison with data can show where assumptions need refinement. The same workflow carries from mechanical systems to circuits, fluids, and heat transfer. Course objectives and assessment

title: Math Review
summary: Review integration, vector operations, and complex numbers used in dynamic modeling.
text: Integration and derivatives A derivative describes an instantaneous rate. Integration accumulates that rate, so the change in a quantity between two times is the integral of its rate over that interval. The integration constant sets the initial position. Worked example · From velocity to position A cart starts at 2 m and travels at 3 m/s for 2 s. Integrating the velocity gives a change of 6 m. Adding that change to the initial position gives a final position of 8 m. Use substitution when an integrand contains a function and its derivative. Use integration by parts when differentiating one factor simplifies a product. For definite integrals, also transform the limits if you change variables. Vectors and fields The dot product gives the component of one vector along another direction, scaled by the vector lengths. Work is the line integral of force dotted with displacement. The cross product gives a perpendicular vector and is used in the moment \(\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\). A scalar triple product gives signed volume. Its sign changes when two vectors are exchanged. The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of a scalar field. Divergence describes local net outflow, and curl describes local circulation. The divergence theorem relates flux through a closed surface to the volume integral of divergence. Stokes’ theorem relates circulation around an oriented boundary to the surface integral of curl. Connect the math to a machine. A horizontal 10 N force applied 0.20 m above a shaft has a 2 N·m moment magnitude. Sliding its line of action through the shaft makes the moment zero even though the force magnitude stays 10 N. Watch the moment arm change on a pinned rod. Complex numbers Write a complex number as \(a+jb\) or in magnitude–phase form. Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), and its phase is \(\operatorname{atan2}(b,a)\). Multiplication adds phases and multiplies magnitudes. Euler’s formula turns a complex exponential into sine and cosine, which is how conjugate roots lead to a real oscillatory response. Imagine the complex point \(z=e^{(-1+2j)t}\). Its distance from the origin is \(e^{-t}\) while its angle increases by 2 rad each second. Its horizontal projection is the real displacement \(e^{-t}\cos(2t)\). When you see a complex root later, sketch the shrinking radius and then project the rotating point onto a line.

title: First-Order Systems
summary: Use equilibria, time constants, phase lines, and linearization to predict first-order motion.
text: Solve the constant-input model For \(\dot{x}+ax=b\) with constant \(b\) and \(a>0\), the equilibrium is \(x_e=b/a\). Subtracting \(x_e\) gives \(\frac{d}{dt}(x-x_e)=-a(x-x_e)\). The response is [x(t)=x_e+\bigl(x(0)-x_e\bigr)e^{-at}.] The first term is the steady value and the exponential term is the transient. The time constant \(\tau=1/a\) is the time it takes the error to fall to \(1/e\) of its initial value. One time constant therefore completes about 63% of the change to equilibrium. Larger \(\tau\) means a slower response. Explore the time constant Predict. How will a larger time constant affect the rise to the same final value? Try. Compare the three presets. Look for the time at which each curve first reaches approximately 0.63. Model used in the simulation τ x′ + x = 1, with x(0) = 0. x(t) = 1 − exp(−t/τ). Time constant τ FastReferenceSlow Reset Time response Solid line: selected case. Dashed line: starting case. System poles A larger time constant moves the pole toward the origin and slows the decay of the transient. Explain. What changes in the initial slope and the time to reach equilibrium? Why does the final value stay the same? Compare reference plots and values Time constantResponse at t = 1 s 0.5 s0.8651 s0.6322 s0.393 Read a time constant from a measurement Set the final value to one and start at zero. A measurement of 0.632 at 2 s suggests \(\tau=2\) s. Check a second point: at 1 s the model predicts \(1-e^{-1/2}\approx0.393\). Open the two-second time-constant case and compare the numerical readout. If you repeated the measurement on a thermometer with a nonzero initial temperature, first subtract the initial reading and divide by the total rise. Phase lines and local linearization For \(\dot{x}=f(x)\), an equilibrium satisfies \(f(x_e)=0\). Draw arrows to the right where \(f\) is positive and to the left where \(f\) is negative. Arrows pointing in on both sides indicate local attraction. With \(\delta x=x-x_e\), the linearization is \(\frac{d}{dt}\delta x\approx f'(x_e)\delta x\). A negative derivative gives local asymptotic stability and a positive derivative gives instability. If the derivative is zero, inspect the nonlinear terms or the phase line. Worked example · Classify three equilibria For \(\dot{x}=x-x^3\), factor \(x(1-x^2)=0\) to get equilibria at \(-1\), \(0\), and \(+1\). The slope \(f'(x)=1-3x^2\) is negative at \(\pm1\) and positive at zero. Small disturbances decay near \(\pm1\) and grow near zero. title: Second-Order Systems
summary: Connect characteristic roots to the free response of a mass–spring–damper system.
text: From an ODE to its roots A second-order model needs two initial conditions, typically displacement \(x(0)\) and velocity \(\dot{x}(0)\). For the homogeneous equation \(a\ddot{x}+b\dot{x}+cx=0\), substitute the trial solution \(x=Ce^{st}\). Differentiation introduces factors of \(s\) and \(s^2\). Cancel the common nonzero exponential to obtain \(as^2+bs+c=0\). Characteristic roots Real-valued free response Two distinct real roots \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) \(C_1e^{s_1t}+C_2e^{s_2t}\) Repeated root \(s\) \((C_1+C_2t)e^{st}\) Conjugate roots \(\alpha\pm j\beta\) \(e^{\alpha t}[C_1\cos(\beta t)+C_2\sin(\beta t)]\) The initial conditions determine \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). For a conjugate pair, \(\alpha\) governs the envelope and \(\beta\) gives the angular frequency. Negative real parts give decay, positive real parts give growth, and a purely imaginary nonzero pair produces sustained oscillation. Build a mass–spring–damper model The spring and damper experience the same displacement from the wall. Measure positive displacement to the right from equilibrium. Take positive displacement \(x\) to the right and measure it from equilibrium. The spring contributes \(-kx\) and the viscous damper contributes \(-c\dot{x}\). Newton’s second law gives [m\ddot{x}+c\dot{x}+kx=f(t).] Here \(m\) is in kg, \(c\) in N·s/m, and \(k\) in N/m. Set \(f(t)=0\) for free response. Dividing by \(m\) gives \(\ddot{x}+2\beta\dot{x}+\omega_n^2x=0\), where \(\beta=c/(2m)\) is the damping rate and \(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\) is the undamped natural frequency. The damping ratio \(\zeta=\beta/\omega_n\) is dimensionless, and the roots are \(s=-\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2-\omega_n^2}\). Damping ratio What to expect \(\zeta=0\) Sustained oscillation at \(\omega_n\) \(0<\zeta<1\) Decaying oscillation at \(\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\) \(\zeta=1\) Repeated root at \(-\omega_n\), at the boundary between oscillatory and non-oscillatory behavior \(\zeta>1\) Two negative real roots. The slower mode can dominate the return to equilibrium. Explore damping and free response Predict. Which damping cases will cross equilibrium? If you increase spring stiffness and hold the damper fixed, will the poles move left, right, or farther from the real axis? Try. Compare the damping presets. Switch to damping coefficient to change m, c, and k independently. Move one slider at a time and watch the roots move. Model used in the simulation m x″ + c x′ + kx = 0. ωₙ = √(k/m), and ζ = c/[2√(mk)]. Initial displacement is 0.10 m and the initial velocity is zero. Pull the mass 0.10 m to the right and release it from rest. What displacement will you measure as it returns toward equilibrium? For \(\ddot{x}+4\dot{x}+5x=0\), the roots are \(-2\pm j\). With \(x(0)=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(\dot{x}(0)=0\), evaluating the response and its derivative at \(t=0\) gives \(C_1=0.10\) and \(C_2=0.20\). The resulting displacement is \[x(t)=0.10e^{-2t}\bigl(\cos t+2\sin t\bigr)\ \mathrm{m}.\] Run these exact values in the cart simulation. A release from 1 m scales every displacement by ten and gives the same roots. Its envelope decays at \(2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and its period is \(2\pi\,\mathrm{s}\). For comparison, \(\ddot{x}+6\dot{x}+9x=0\) has the repeated root \(-3\), so its free response has the form \((C_1+C_2t)e^{-3t}\). The equation \(\ddot{x}-4\dot{x}+3x=0\) has positive roots at \(1\) and \(3\), so a nonzero mode grows. From free to forced response Free response isolates the effect of initial displacement and velocity. The quarter-car problem introduces road motion as an input, so the forcing frequency matters too. In Assignment 2, identify which part of the solution decays and which part remains while the road input continues. When does a mount isolate vibration? Imagine a machine mounted on a vibrating floor. The floor moves through a fixed amplitude \(Y\) while the forcing frequency \(\omega\) changes. How large is the machine’s absolute displacement \(X\) after the transient dies away? The spring and damper connect the mass to the moving floor. With upward displacement positive for both, their forces depend on relative motion. Newton’s law gives [m\ddot x+c(\dot x-\dot y)+k(x-y)=0.] For sinusoidal base motion, the steady displacement amplitude ratio is [T=\frac{X}{Y}=\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}},\qquad r=\frac{\omega}{\omega_n}.] At low frequency the mass follows the floor. Near resonance it can travel farther than the floor. Above \(r=\sqrt{2}\), the mass displacement amplitude is smaller than the base amplitude. This criterion applies to the steady sinusoidal displacement comparison. Test a vibration isolator Predict. If the floor moves through 10 mm, can the machine move more than 10 mm? Try. Change the driving frequency. Compare steady floor and machine motion, then locate the selected case on the amplitude-ratio curve. Compare that answer with the resonant case. Reference case For a 1 kg machine and a 16 N/m mount the natural frequency is 4 rad/s. At a frequency ratio of √2 the two amplitudes are equal for either damping setting. How would a vibration absorber differ? An isolator changes the transmission path from the floor. A tuned absorber adds a second moving mass. In the ideal undamped, force-driven case, tune its spring and mass so that \(\sqrt{k_a/m_a}\) equals the forcing frequency. The absorber can then supply the opposing spring force while the primary mass has zero steady harmonic displacement. Detuning and damping change that result. Two applications from the lecture Pendulum and humanoid balance. Near the hanging position, the small-angle, undamped model satisfies \(\ddot{\theta}+(g/\ell)\theta=0\). Near the upright position, the sign changes to \(\ddot{\theta}-(g/\ell)\theta=0\). The first model has purely imaginary roots and bounded oscillations. The upright model has a positive root and a growing mode, which explains why a standing robot needs a means of stabilizing its motion. Passive quarter-car. A one-mass model captures one mode. Adding independent body and wheel motion introduces a second mass and four states. The suspension forces depend on the relative body and wheel motion. The tire spring depends on the difference between wheel displacement and road height. Lecture 14 develops the coupled equations.

title: Laplace Transforms
summary: Carry initial conditions into an algebraic equation in s and recover the time response.
text: Transform the equation and the initial conditions The unilateral Laplace transform weights \(x(t)\) by \(e^{-st}\) and integrates from \(0\) to \(\infty\). For derivatives, the initial conditions enter as [\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}{\dot{x}} &= sX-x(0), \mathcal{L}{\ddot{x}} &= s^2X-sx(0)-\dot{x}(0). \end{aligned}] These initial-condition terms distinguish the full response from a transfer-function calculation. Useful pairs include \(\mathcal{L}\{1\}=1/s\), \(\mathcal{L}\{e^{-at}\}=1/(s+a)\), and \(\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\omega/(s^2+\omega^2)\). A delay of \(T\) with a causal switch multiplies the transform by \(e^{-sT}\). Solve and invert Worked example · Recover the time response For \(\dot{x}+2x=4\) and \(x(0)=1\), the transform gives \((s+2)X=4/s+1\). Decompose \(X=2/s-1/(s+2)\) and invert to get \(x(t)=2-e^{-2t}\). The initial value and equilibrium verify the signs. Distinct poles give sums of exponentials. A repeated factor \(1/(s+a)^2\) gives \(te^{-at}\). For a conjugate pair, complete the square and split the numerator so it matches shifted sine and cosine transforms. Work through a Laplace solution Define velocity as positive to the right. The applied force is six newtons and the damper opposes the motion. Given. A 1 kg mass slides on a frictionless surface. The damper coefficient is 3 N·s/m, the applied step force is 6 N to the right, and the initial velocity is 1 m/s to the right. Predict. Which term carries the initial value into the transformed equation? Try. Use the free-body diagram to write the velocity equation. Select the transform of the derivative, then reveal each step when you have tried it yourself. If V(s) is the transform of velocity, what is the transform of its derivative? sV sV − 1 sV + 1 Check prediction Check your predictionThe unilateral derivative rule subtracts the initial value. Step 1 · Write the force balance Positive force acts to the right and the damper opposes velocity. Applied force minus damping force equals mass times acceleration, so v′ + 3v = 6 with v(0) = 1. Step 2 · Transform the ODE Subtract the initial value from the derivative term and collect the terms in V. (s + 3)V = 6/s + 1. Step 3 · Split into simple fractions Write the transformed response as a steady contribution and a decaying contribution. V = 2/s − 1/(s + 3). Step 4 · Invert and check At time zero the response is 1. As time increases, it approaches 2. v(t) = 2 − exp(−3t) m/s. Explain. Check that the solution has the given initial value and approaches the equilibrium implied by the original equation. Watch the two forces come into balance Predict. What happens to the net force as the cart speeds up? Try. Play the solved response with the initial velocity of 1 m/s. Compare the force arrows and readouts as the cart approaches 2 m/s. Play Step Reset Time 0.00 s Cart motion and horizontal forces The orange applied-force arrow stays fixed. The green damping force grows as speed rises. Explain. Explain how a cart with nearly zero net force can keep moving. Reference case At release, the 6 N applied force opposes a 3 N damper force, leaving 3 N net. At steady speed, both force magnitudes approach 6 N.

title: Convolution and System Response
summary: Find the output of a linear time-invariant model by accumulating shifted impulse responses.
text: What does one earlier tap contribute? Imagine giving the cart a quick push to the right with your fingertip and immediately letting go. That brief contact is the tap. Its impulse \(J=\int F(t)\,dt\) is the area under the force–time curve. For example, a 100 N force applied for 0.01 s delivers \(1\,\mathrm{N\,s}\) of impulse. In the demo, the contact is so short compared with one oscillation that we model it as instantaneous. The 1 kg cart starts at rest at equilibrium. A rightward impulse of \(1\,\mathrm{N\,s}\) increases its velocity by \(\Delta v=J/m=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Its position is continuous through the tap. Once contact ends, the spring and damper govern the motion. Tap the cart at 0 s and again at 1 s. Pause at 3 s. The first response is three seconds old, so it contributes \(J h(3)\) to the displacement. The second is two seconds old, so it contributes \(J h(2)\). Here \(h\) gives displacement per unit impulse after that much time has elapsed. Both taps pushed to the right. Can one contribution now point left? Add two taps Predict. At 3 s, will both taps move the cart to the same side of equilibrium? Try. Start with the first tap. Add a second tap at 1 s, then scrub to 3 s. Read the two displacements and their sum. Second unit impulse First tap only Second tap at 1 s Second tap at 2 s Play Step Reset Time 0.00 s Displacement due to each tap and their sum Purple is the first tap. Dashed green is the second. Dotted orange is their sum. Explain. Which contribution changes if you delay only the second tap? Reference case A later tap has the same response shape shifted to its arrival time. At 3 s the first tap contributes negatively and the tap at 1 s contributes positively. Now divide a sustained force into slices. A slice at past time \(\tau\) delivers impulse \(F(\tau)\Delta\tau\). At the observation time \(t\) its displacement contribution is approximately \(F(\tau)\Delta\tau\,h(t-\tau)\). Sum the slices and shrink their widths to obtain the integral below. From an impulse to an arbitrary input A linear time-invariant system’s impulse response \(h(t)\) describes its zero-state response to a unit impulse. Linearity lets us scale a contribution by the input value and add contributions. Time invariance lets us shift \(h\) by the time at which the contribution is applied. For causal signals and zero initial conditions, [y(t)=\int_0^t h(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau.] The term \(h(t-\tau)\) describes the amount of response left at \(t\) from input applied at \(\tau\). The Laplace-domain relation is \(Y(s)=H(s)U(s)\). For the mass–spring–damper system, take \(u=F\) and \(y=x\). The impulse response \(h(t)\) describes the displacement caused by one unit of impulse area. The integral adds the displacement contributions from all earlier portions of the force. The spring and damper cause the motion to oscillate and decay. Displacement is the signed area of force times the shifted impulse response. The impulse response is zero at negative times. Compare a step, an ideal impulse, and two finite pulses on this same mass. Worked response to a two-second push Let \(g(t)\) be the displacement produced by a sustained 1 N step on this same mass. It is the accumulated impulse response \(g(t)=\int_0^t h(\lambda)\,d\lambda\) for \(t\geq0\), and zero for \(t<0\). A 1 N force that turns off at 2 s is a positive step at time zero and a negative step at 2 s. Linearity and time shifting give \[x(t)=g(t)-g(t-2).\] Before 2 s, only the first term contributes. After 2 s, the force is zero and the two displacement responses continue to combine. This gives the same result as integrating \(F(\tau)h(t-\tau)\) over the time the force was applied. For nonzero initial conditions, add the free response separately. Check the endpoints For an ordinary initial displacement with no impulse in the displacement signal, \(x(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}sX(s)\). For a rational transform, if all poles of \(sX(s)\) lie strictly in the left half-plane, \(x(\infty)=\lim_{s\to0}sX(s)\). The resting, damped cart returns to zero after a finite push. title: Transfer Functions and Stability
summary: Derive an input-to-output transfer function and use its poles to interpret the response.
text: Pick the input and output first A transfer function is the ratio of a chosen output transform to a chosen input transform when the system starts from rest. Once you know the block \(G(s)\), you can use it with different inputs through \(Y(s)=G(s)U(s)\). Read displacement at the branch and velocity after multiplying by s. Both outputs come from the same applied force. Take the Laplace transform of \(m\ddot{x}+c\dot{x}+kx=f\) with zero initial displacement and velocity. Group the terms multiplying \(X(s)\), then divide by the force input. [\begin{aligned} (ms^2+cs+k)X(s)&=F(s), \frac{X(s)}{F(s)}&=\frac{1}{ms^2+cs+k},& \frac{V(s)}{F(s)}&=\frac{s}{ms^2+cs+k}. \end{aligned}] The velocity block uses \(V(s)=sX(s)\) because the initial position is zero. For the two outputs drawn here, the numerator changes while the denominator stays the same. Trace how the spring and damper produce that denominator. Connect poles to modes After reducing the rational expression, the roots of the denominator are its poles. A pole on the negative real axis gives a decaying exponential, and a conjugate pair with negative real parts gives decaying oscillation. For a proper rational transfer function, bounded-input bounded-output stability requires all poles to lie strictly in the open left half-plane. A canceled mode can still matter internally, so check the state model when internal stability is the question. The push and tap below use fixed mass, stiffness, and damping. In Second-Order Systems, change those parameters to see how the model’s poles move. Add the input The type of input determines what you multiply the same block by. A force step of magnitude \(F_0\) gives \(F(s)=F_0/s\). An ideal impulse of area \(J\) gives \(F(s)=J\). In both cases, compute \(X(s)=[X(s)/F(s)]F(s)\). Worked example · Check the final displacement At rest, both acceleration and velocity are zero. The spring balances the applied force, so the final displacement is \(F_0/k\). A 1 N push on a 16 N/m spring gives \(1/16=0.0625\,\mathrm{m}\), or 62.5 mm. An ideal impulse with area \(J\) transfers momentum without an instantaneous change in position. Integrating the force balance across the tap gives \(m[v(0^+)-v(0^-)]=J\). After the tap, the mass moves freely under the spring and damper forces. The transfer function’s impulse response \(h(t)\) is the displacement per unit impulse area. A push and a tap Take the positive x direction to the right. Weight and the normal reaction balance vertically. Given. The mass starts at equilibrium and at rest, and positive displacement is to the right. Predict. What happens if you keep pushing the mass? What changes if you only tap it once? Try. Start with a 1 N step and watch the mass settle. Then select the ideal impulse and two short pulses. Both short pulses supply 1 N·s of impulse. Compare their motion with the ideal tap. title: Exam 1 Review
summary: Practice moving between ODEs, equilibria, Laplace transforms, and time responses.
text: Test yourself Try each problem on paper before opening the hint or solution. Predict the direction A sensor starts above its steady reading. Sketch its stable first-order response to a constant input. Could it cross the steady value? Hint Write the error as \(e=x-x_e\). Check the reasoning The error obeys \(\dot e=-e/\tau\). Its sign stays positive, so the reading falls monotonically toward equilibrium. Revisit the lecture example. Calculate a response A resting cart has \(\dot v+2v=u\). A unit step is applied. Find the impulse response and use it to obtain the velocity at 1 s. Hint Take \(V/U\) with zero initial velocity. Integrate the impulse response over the past second. Check the reasoning The impulse response is \(h(t)=e^{-2t}\) for \(t\geq0\). Its integral gives \(v(1)=(1-e^{-2})/2\approx0.432\) in the chosen velocity units. Revisit the lecture example. Diagnose a damping claim A classmate says a 1 kg cart with \(k=9\) N/m and \(c=4\) N·s/m must be overdamped because the damping coefficient exceeds one. What do the roots say? Hint Use \(c^2-4mk\) or compute the dimensionless damping ratio. Check the reasoning The discriminant is \(16-36=-20\). The poles are \(-2\pm j\sqrt5\) per second and the motion is underdamped. The critical coefficient is 6 N·s/m. Revisit the lecture example. A modeling and analysis sequence State the input, response, initial conditions, and units. For a first-order model, solve for its equilibrium and compare the initial state to that equilibrium. For a second-order model, derive the characteristic equation and classify its roots before solving for constants. Choose a solution route Use the direct ODE method for free response or simple constant inputs. Use Laplace transforms when a forced input or initial conditions make the time-domain algebra less convenient. Use convolution when the impulse response and input history are known. Derive a transfer function under zero initial conditions, then apply the input separately. Check your result Worked example · Check a first-order response For \(\dot{x}+3x=6\) with \(x(0)=0\), the equilibrium is \(2\) and the time constant is \(1/3\,\mathrm{s}\). Predict the sign of the initial slope before solving. The solution \(x(t)=2(1-e^{-3t})\) begins at zero, has initial slope \(6\), and approaches \(2\). For a nonlinear model, locate equilibria first and only then linearize about the equilibrium of interest.

title: Rigid-Body Dynamics
summary: Apply force, moment, and energy balances to derive equations of motion.
text: Start with a free-body diagram Choose a system boundary and positive directions. Account for applied forces, weight, reactions, and friction. For planar rigid-body motion, apply \(\sum\mathbf{F}=m\mathbf{a}_G\) to the center of mass and \(\sum M_G=I_G\alpha\) about it. For rotation about a fixed axis, the moment of inertia about that axis can be found with \(I_O=I_G+md^2\). Work through a moment balance Measure the angle from the downward vertical. The pin reactions pass through O. The weight’s lever arm is the horizontal distance from O to its line of action. Given. A uniform 2 kg rod is 1.2 m long and pinned at one end. Release it from rest at 30° from the downward vertical. Its center of mass is 0.60 m from the pin. Predict. Where does the weight of a uniform rod act when you take moments about its pin? Try. Identify the weight’s line of action and its perpendicular distance from the pin. The pin reactions pass through the pivot, so they make no moment about it. Then work through the balance. What is the perpendicular lever arm of the weight? L L sin θ (L/2) sin θ Check prediction Check your predictionThe center of mass is halfway along the rod. The perpendicular distance to the weight’s line of action is the horizontal offset. Step 1 · Write the moment of gravity Define positive angle away from the downward vertical in the direction of the initial displacement. Gravity acts to reduce that positive angle. Moment about the pin = −mg(L/2)sin θ. Step 2 · Use the inertia about the pin The moment of inertia of the uniform rod about its pinned end is 0.96 kg·m². I about the pin = mL²/3 = 0.96 kg·m². The model neglects pivot friction. Energy and friction For a particle or rigid body, work changes kinetic energy. With conservative forces represented by potential energy, work by the remaining forces changes the sum of kinetic and potential energy. Static friction supplies the force required to avoid slip until its limiting magnitude is reached. During sliding, kinetic friction opposes the relative velocity. Pendulum example The link force passes through the pivot. Gravity supplies the moment about the pivot. For a point mass on a massless link, moment balance about the pivot gives \(m\ell^2\ddot{\theta}=-mg\ell\sin\theta\). Near the downward equilibrium, \(\sin\theta\approx\theta\) for \(\theta\) in radians, so \(\ddot{\theta}+(g/\ell)\theta\approx0\). The small-angle frequency \(\sqrt{g/\ell}\) follows from the linearized model. Compare the small- and large-angle motion of a lightly damped point pendulum in Phase Portraits and Stability.

title: Drive Kinematics
summary: Model pulleys, belts, and gear pairs with kinematic constraints and torque balances.
text: No slip links rotation and translation At a pulley of radius \(r\), no slip gives a rim speed \(r\omega\) and tangential acceleration \(r\alpha\). A belt or cable transmits this motion to a connected component. Select signs from the actual direction of motion. Write separate force balances for the translating bodies and a moment balance for the pulley. If the pulley has inertia, tensions can differ on opposite sides. From drum to load. A cable winds without slip on a drum of radius \(r\). Its load speed is \(v=r\omega\), and a cable tension \(T\) exerts a moment of magnitude \(Tr\). The reflected inertia of a translating mass follows from energy: \(\tfrac12 mv^2=\tfrac12(mr^2)\omega^2\). This lets one angular balance include both drum and load. Gear speed, torque, and inertia The pitch circles have the same tangential speed at contact. The gear with fewer teeth turns faster. Meshing external gears have equal tangential speed magnitude at their pitch point and rotate in opposite directions. For tooth counts \(N_1\) and \(N_2\), \(\omega_2/\omega_1=-N_1/N_2\). In an ideal lossless pair, torque magnitude varies inversely with speed magnitude. For a load inertia \(J_2\), its value reflected to shaft 1 is \(J_2(\omega_2/\omega_1)^2\). The square follows by equating kinetic energies. Worked example · A 24-tooth gear drives a 12-tooth gear With the driver turning at 2 rad/s, the driven speed is \(-2(24/12)=-4\,\mathrm{rad/s}\). The negative sign marks opposite rotation. In the ideal pair, the output torque magnitude is half the input torque magnitude. Follow the motion of meshing gears Predict. title: Springs and State Space
summary: Build spring models and express a second-order ODE as a first-order state model.
text: Spring force and energy In parallel, the springs share displacement. In series, they carry the same force. A linear spring exerts a restoring force proportional to displacement from its unstretched length. Two springs in parallel share displacement and their stiffnesses add. Springs in series share force, so their compliances add. An ideal spring stores energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2\). Spring and damper in series. For a massless junction the transmitted force is common. The total extension is \(x=x_s+x_d\), where \(x_s=F/k\) and \(\dot x_d=F/c\). Differentiating gives \(\dot x=\dot F/k+F/c\). If total extension is held fixed, the force relaxes with time constant \(c/k\). This differs from parallel elements, which share the same extension. From an ODE to state equations Worked example · Choose states for a spring–mass system Choose position \(x\) and velocity \(v\) as the states for \(m\ddot{x}+kx=f\). The two equations are \(\dot{x}=v\) and \(\dot{v}=-(k/m)x+f/m\). In the form \(\dot{z}=Az+Bu\) and \(y=Cz+Du\), the position output uses \(C=[1,\;0]\) and \(D=0\). Choose the output from the physical measurement of interest. Coupled motion A spring between two masses acts on their relative displacement and exerts equal and opposite forces. A normal mode describes a shape in which the masses oscillate at one frequency with fixed displacement ratios. Energy alternates between kinetic energy and spring energy in the undamped model. Two masses, two modes Predict. Which motion stretches the spring between the masses? Try. Play the in-phase and out-of-phase releases, then try the mixture. Pause to compare the direction of motion of each mass. Starting motion In-phase Out-of-phase Mixed motion Play Step Reset Time 0.00 s Coupled mass motion Purple is mass 1. Orange is mass 2. The motion is exaggerated for visibility. Mass displacements over time Solid purple is mass 1. Dashed orange is mass 2. Explain. Which pure mode oscillates faster? Explain the difference by looking at the center spring. Reference case For equal masses of 1 kg, outer springs of 9 N/m, and a coupling spring of 8 N/m, the in-phase frequency is 3 rad/s and the out-of-phase frequency is 5 rad/s. The mixed release combines these two modes.

title: Dampers and State Space
summary: Use force laws and state equations to distinguish storage, dissipation, and measured outputs.
text: Where energy goes The spring and damper experience the same displacement from the wall. Measure positive displacement to the right from equilibrium. An ideal viscous damper produces force proportional to relative velocity. For a damper connected to ground, \(F_d=-cv\). Its power acting on the mass is \(-cv^2\), so it dissipates mechanical energy when \(c>0\). A spring stores energy and can return it to the mass. Worked example · Find the force and power For a damper of 2 N·s/m and a cart moving right at 1 m/s, the damper force on the cart is \(F_d=-2\,\mathrm{N}\). Its power on the cart is \(F_dv=-2\,\mathrm{W}\), so the damper removes mechanical energy at 2 W. First isolate the damper by removing the spring. Compare a cart that coasts from an initial speed with one that is pushed from rest. The animation follows the position, while the plots show speed and the rate of energy loss. Follow the force and energy loss in a damper Predict. If you double the damping coefficient, what happens to the speed of a coasting cart? Try. Play the coast case and change the damping coefficient. Then apply the 2 N step and compare the steady speed. The green arrow is the force the damper exerts on the cart. Cart input Coast from 1 m/s Apply 2 N from rest Damping coefficient 1 N·s/m 2 N·s/m 4 N·s/m Play Step Reset Time 0.00 s Cart velocity The purple curve follows velocity on the positive axis. Power dissipated The green curve shows the rate at which the damper removes mechanical energy. Cart and viscous damper The green force arrow opposes the cart’s motion. The applied push Explain. In the driven case, how can the cart move at constant speed while the damper still dissipates energy? Reference case At 2 N·s/m, a 2 N push gives a steady speed of 1 m/s. At that speed the damper dissipates 2 W and the applied force supplies 2 W. The damper force opposes motion. Dissipated power is positive and equals the damping coefficient times speed squared. In Second-Order Systems, use damping coefficient mode to hold mass and stiffness fixed while you find the critical damping threshold. Model and measurement For position \(x\) and velocity \(v\), \(\dot{x}=v\) and \(\dot{v}=(f-cv-kx)/m\). A position or velocity output selects one state directly. An acceleration output uses coefficients \(-k/m\) and \(-c/m\) on the states and has a direct feedthrough term \(f/m\). Compare free and forced response The state equations accommodate either an initial displacement or a time-varying force. The homogeneous motion depends on the eigenvalues. The forced motion also depends on the input.

title: Transfer Functions and Block Diagrams
summary: Translate force balances into integrator blocks and trace the signals to an output.
text: Build from the highest derivative For \(m\ddot{x}+c\dot{x}+kx=f\), use a summing point to combine \(f\), \(-c\dot{x}\), and \(-kx\). A gain \(1/m\) gives acceleration. Integrate once to obtain velocity and again to obtain displacement. Return position and velocity through the spring and damper gains. In the first diagram, follow the top row left to right. The lower summing junction adds the spring and damper terms, and the upper junction subtracts their sum from the applied force. A filled dot copies a signal into a branch. The blocks marked \(1/s\) integrate under zero initial conditions. The lower junction adds the spring and damper terms. The upper junction subtracts their sum from the applied force. From integrators to a transfer function Take the positive x direction to the right. Weight and the normal reaction balance vertically. Given. The mass starts at rest at equilibrium. Take displacement and applied force as positive to the right. Predict. If we replace the full block diagram with a single transfer function, what should happen to the displacement curve? Try. The green buttons highlight the signals that feed your selection. The forward block combines the mass gain and two integrators. The feedback block combines the spring and damper. The reduced block maps force to displacement with zero initial conditions. For negative feedback, \(X/F=G/(1+GH)\). Substituting the two blocks gives the equivalent transfer function. The plot overlays its displacement with the full integrator model using the same input and timeline. Mass–spring–damper motion The mass follows the same force and timeline as the block diagram. Both feedback forces initially vanish. The displacement curves from the integrators and the reduced transfer function agree throughout the run. Mass is 1 kg, damping is 2.4 N·s/m, and the spring stiffness is 16 N/m. The net force is the applied force plus the two feedback forces. Read the diagram as algebra Worked example · Reduce the feedback loop The three forward blocks multiply to \(G=1/(ms^2)\). Since \(V=sX\), the two feedback branches combine to \(cV+kX=(cs+k)X\). That makes \(H=cs+k\). The input to the forward block is therefore \(F-HX\), the force shown at the minus summing junction. \[\begin{aligned} X&=G(F-HX),\\ (1+GH)X&=GF,\\ \frac{X}{F}&=\frac{G}{1+GH}=\frac{1}{ms^2+cs+k}. \end{aligned}\] The reduced block maps force to displacement with zero initial conditions. title: Coupled Systems and the Quarter-Car Model
summary: Connect relative spring and damper forces to a two-mass dynamic model.
text: Write each mass balance separately Use the same positive direction for the two displacements. Between masses with displacements \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), a linear spring contributes \(-k(x_1-x_2)\) on mass 1 and the opposite force on mass 2. A damper similarly uses the velocity difference. Explicit relative terms make the signs easier to check. A passive quarter-car Let \(z_s\) be body displacement, \(z_u\) wheel displacement, and \(r\) road height. The suspension spring and damper depend on \(z_s-z_u\) and its derivative. A simple tire spring applies \(k_t(r-z_u)\) to the unsprung mass. Measure displacement from static equilibrium so constant weight is already balanced by the static deflections. Worked example · Find the suspension force Hold the body at equilibrium and raise the wheel 10 mm. At an instant when both velocities are zero, only the spring contributes to the suspension force. With a stiffness of 16,500 N/m, it pushes up on the body with 165 N and down on the wheel with 165 N. The free-body diagrams give [m_s\ddot z_s=-S,\qquad m_u\ddot z_u=S+k_t(r-z_u).] Add the equations. The suspension force cancels because it is internal to the body–wheel pair. A sign error leaves an extra suspension force in the sum. To get this passive model from the lecture PDF’s general model, set the actuator force and tire damping coefficient to zero. The suspension damper still acts between body and wheel. From equations to outputs The two second-order equations require four states: both positions and both velocities. To obtain a transfer function, transform the two equations under zero initial conditions and solve for the chosen output. title: Phase Portraits and Stability
summary: Relate equilibria, linearization, eigenvalues, and the geometry of trajectories.
text: Find the equilibria first For \(\dot{z}=f(z,u)\) with fixed input \(\bar{u}\), an equilibrium \(z_e\) satisfies \(f(z_e,\bar{u})=0\). The Jacobian \(A\) at that point maps small displacements in state to first-order changes in the dynamics. The linearized system describes nearby motion. Large perturbations can expose nonlinear behavior absent from the linear model. At the hanging equilibrium of a damped simple pendulum, use angular displacement \(\theta\) and angular velocity \(\omega\). The local acceleration is \(\dot\omega\approx-(g/\ell)\theta-b\omega\) with \(b>0\). Around the upright position the gravity term reverses sign. A small positive angle with zero initial speed then accelerates farther away. Inspect the arrows on the horizontal axis first. Read the phase portrait Each point represents a full state. The vector field gives the initial direction of motion, and the trajectory follows those directions through time. For two real eigenvalues, the eigendirections describe straight trajectories of a linear model. A saddle has one growing and one decaying direction. A stable focus spirals inward as time advances. Pendulum example The link force passes through the pivot. Gravity supplies the moment about the pivot. The states are angle and angular velocity. The downward and upright equilibria have zero angular velocity but different local dynamics. Near the upright equilibrium, gravity amplifies small departures in an unforced pendulum. Near the downward equilibrium it restores the angle. Positive damping turns small oscillations about the downward equilibrium into decaying motion. Pendulum and phase portrait Predict. For block diagrams, start with the highest derivative and integrate to recover the states. For a transfer function, select one input and one output and impose zero initial conditions. title: Electromechanical Coupling
summary: Predict the force on a current-carrying rod and the voltage across the same rod when it moves.
text: From current to force and motion to voltage Imagine a conducting rod that bridges two horizontal rails and can slide left or right. Define positive current as up the rod and positive motion as to the right. A dot in the diagram means the magnetic field points out of the page, toward you. A cross means it points into the page. Drive the rod with current. Point your right-hand fingers up the rod and curl them toward the field. Your thumb points along the magnetic force \(\mathbf F=i(\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf B)\). With the field toward you and current upward, the force points right. Reverse the current and the rod accelerates left. Move the rod by hand. Disconnect the source and connect an ideal voltmeter across the rails. Push the rod right through the same outward field. A positive charge moving with the rod feels \(q(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\) downward, so positive charge builds up at the bottom. A meter with its positive lead on the bottom rail reads a positive voltage, even with zero current through the meter. The experiment uses a 0.20 m rod of mass 0.25 kg sliding without friction. In the current-driven trial it starts from rest. In the hand-driven trial you set its velocity and the ideal voltmeter draws zero current. Drive the rod or use it as a generator Predict. title: Fluid Systems and Electrical Analogies
summary: Model hydraulic pressure, restrictions, capacitance, and piston forces.
text: Pressure and flow Pressure difference drives volumetric flow in a hydraulic restriction. Near a chosen operating point, a nonlinear relation can be approximated with a local resistance \(R=d(\Delta p)/dq\). Pressure plays a role analogous to voltage, and flow to current. Storage and pressure force For a free-surface tank with \(p=\rho gh\), a constant surface area \(A\) corresponds to fluid capacitance \(C_h=A/(\rho g)\), where \(q_{\mathrm{net}}=C_h\dot{p}\). A piston turns a pressure difference into force. For equal effective areas, \(F=A_p(p_1-p_2)\). For unequal areas, calculate each pressure force separately. Watch how storage and outlet resistance set the response in the two-tank fill and drain example. Coupled actuator model Positive motion increases the left volume and decreases the right volume. Use the effective area for each chamber when finding its pressure force. In a double-acting actuator, piston motion changes the two chamber volumes in opposite directions. Include these volume changes in the chamber flow balances, and use chamber pressures in the piston’s mechanical balance. For a simple damper with \(q=A_pv\) and \(\Delta p=Rq\), the equivalent damping magnitude is \(RA_p^2\). For the sealed-air model, prescribe the piston motion and treat the gas as isothermal. Each chamber obeys \(pV=p_0V_0\). As the piston moves, the gas pressure rises in the shrinking chamber and falls in the expanding chamber. Switch to the open-port liquid model to compare with the flow required by the same motion. title: Thermal Systems
summary: Use energy conservation, thermal resistance, and capacitance to predict temperature.
text: A lumped thermal model The heater adds energy. The thermal resistance governs how quickly heat leaves for a given temperature difference. When a body can be approximated by one temperature, its thermal capacitance is \(C_{\mathrm{th}}=mc_p\). A thermal resistance \(R_{\mathrm{th}}\) relates heat rate to temperature difference. With constant ambient temperature \(T_a\) and heater power \(P\), the energy balance is [C_{\mathrm{th}}\dot{T}=P-\frac{T-T_a}{R_{\mathrm{th}}}.] At steady state the temperature is \(T_a+PR_{\mathrm{th}}\). The time constant is \(R_{\mathrm{th}}C_{\mathrm{th}}\). A model in the deviation \(T-T_a\) looks mathematically like the RC circuit. The animated thermometers share a 20–60 °C scale. title: Connecting System Representations
summary: Explain how ODEs, state space, transfer functions, and phase portraits describe the same dynamics.
text: Separate the model from its representation An ODE states the governing balance. A state model makes the evolving variables explicit. A block diagram exposes how signals and integrations connect. A transfer function describes one input-to-output map under zero initial conditions. For \(\dot{z}=Az+Bu\) and \(y=Cz+Du\), take the Laplace transform with zero initial state to obtain [G(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B+D.] The roots of \(\det(sI-A)\) are eigenvalues. In a minimal realization they also appear as transfer-function poles. Modes that cancel in an input-output map can still appear in the state model. Follow one release through every representation Release a 1 kg mass from 1 m at zero speed. Use \(c=2\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}\) and \(k=5\,\mathrm{N/m}\). There is no applied force after release. How can there be motion when the input is zero? The force balance gives \(\ddot x+2\dot x+5x=f\). Writing \(z=[x,\dot x]^T\) gives [\dot z=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\-5&-2\end{bmatrix}z+\begin{bmatrix}0\1\end{bmatrix}f.] The characteristic roots, eigenvalues, and force-to-position transfer-function poles are all \(-1\pm2j\). With the given initial state the free response is \(x(t)=e^{-t}(\cos 2t+\tfrac12\sin 2t)\) m. The transfer function \(1/(s^2+2s+5)\) describes the separate zero-state response to force. Here the initial spring energy supplies the motion. One clock for motion and state Predict. On which axis does the state lie when the cart reverses direction? Try. Step the clock. Follow the cart, the point on its displacement trace, and the same instant in the phase plane. Play Step Reset Time 0.00 s Spring–mass–damper release The mass starts displaced from equilibrium. No external force acts during the release. Displacement through time A marker follows the free response of the released cart. Velocity versus displacement The marker follows the damped spiral toward equilibrium. Explain. Pause near a displacement extremum. What happens to the velocity and why does the phase curve cross the horizontal axis there? Reference case The cart starts at 1 m with zero velocity. It first turns on the opposite side at about 1.57 s and −0.208 m. Both position and velocity decay toward zero. Can a measurement hide a mode? Take two independent states satisfying \(\dot z_1=-z_1+u\) and \(\dot z_2=-3z_2+u\). Measuring only \(z_1\) gives \(Y/U=1/(s+1)\) even though the state matrix also has eigenvalue \(-3\). Measuring \(z_1+z_2\) reveals both modes. Choosing the sensor is part of choosing the model’s output. title: Introduction to Feedback Control
summary: Use a feedback diagram to explain how a controller changes a system’s response.
text: Trace the loop The controller converts position error into force. The measured position returns to the negative input of the summing junction. A reference describes the desired output. A sensor measures the actual output, and the error is the reference minus the measurement. A controller uses this error to choose the plant input. Disturbances can enter the plant even when the reference is fixed. Close the equations For unity negative feedback, plant \(G(s)\), and controller \(C(s)\), the reference-to-output transfer function is [\frac{C(s)G(s)}{1+C(s)G(s)}.] The characteristic equation after algebraic reduction shows how feedback can change the poles. For \(G(s)=1/(ms^2+cs+k)\) and \(C(s)=K_p\), the closed-loop denominator becomes \(ms^2+cs+k+K_p\). Worked example · Find the steady tracking error At rest, the spring force \(kx\) balances the controller force \(K_p(r-x)\). If both stiffness and proportional gain are 16 N/m, a 1 m command settles at \(x=K_pr/(k+K_p)=0.5\,\mathrm m\). The remaining 0.5 m error keeps the controller pushing against the spring. title: Course Overview
text: ME 3050 · 3 credits Modeling and Analysis of Dynamic Systems Model physical systems, predict their response, and test what your models can explain. Course Description This course presents techniques for developing and analyzing models of mechanical, electrical, electromechanical, fluid and thermal systems. Transient, steady-state and frequency response are determined using analytical and numerical methods. Covers tools for stability analysis and state-space representation. Covers linear free- and forced-vibrations in single- and multi-degree-of-freedom systems with lumped-parameters representation, methods of vibration absorption and isolations.
